DIESEL stress-tested as simultaneous wars target refineries

Global prices for diesel and other middle distillates remain close to record highs in real terms as simultaneous conflicts in the Middle East and Russia continue to disrupt refinery operations and export routes.

The wars have become increasingly interconnected, damaging some refineries, while leaving others unable to maintain normal output because they cannot source enough crude and other feedstocks, or export fuels they have produced.

Global refinery capacity has been effectively reduced by as much as 10%, according to some estimates, creating an acute shortage of fuels, rapid depletion of inventories, and intense upward pressure on prices ...

Europe will release 42 million barrels of oil reserves into the market over the next three months as part of its commitment to ease prices, France’s economy minister Roland Lescure said Thursday.

Half of that release will be diesel, Lescure said ahead of a meeting of European Union energy ministers in Luxembourg. Group of Seven nations agreed last month to release up to 100 million barrels, marking a completion of an IEA-coordinated 400-million-barrel release in March.

Lescure said a French release of 10 million barrels of diesel announced last month would hit the market in the coming days and the impact on prices would be felt as soon as next week. The reserves would be supplied to the market at cost price, lowering prices by 12 cents to 18 cents a liter he said.

Natural gas/LNG: With Qatar's LNG production still largely offline and shipments through the Strait of Hormuz facing elevated risks, competition between Europe and Asia for available seaborne supplies continues to intensify. European benchmark gas prices have surged 250% year-to-date, while the Japan/Korea LNG marker has gained 237%, with both now trading well above USD 30 per MMBtu. In Europe, TTF futures briefly exceeded EUR 100 per MWh on Wednesday for the first time since 2022, reviving concerns about another damaging energy price shock.

The latest surge reflects a combination of constrained global LNG supply, unusually low European inventories and growing uncertainty over weather-dependent winter heating demand. A slow rebuilding of storage levels during the summer has left Europe with a substantial supply deficit compared with recent years, equivalent to more than 100 standard-sized LNG carriers. This reduced buffer leaves the region particularly vulnerable to prolonged cold spells or further disruptions to global LNG flows, while forcing European buyers to compete more aggressively with Asian importers for flexible cargoes.

The return to triple-digit gas prices is adding pressure on businesses, households and governments, raising the risk of renewed industrial demand destruction, and persistent inflation. With limited scope for a rapid recovery in Qatari exports, the market is increasingly dependent on demand adjustments and the ability of other LNG producers to redirect supply. Until the geopolitical outlook improves or European inventories recover, gas prices are likely to remain highly sensitive to weather forecasts, shipping disruptions and shifts in Asian demand.

Gold is staging a modest rebound after hitting an early-session low of USD 4,036, as traders digest the latest Fed decision and conclude that monetary policy has entered a wait-and-see phase, with the next move increasingly dependent on incoming economic data. Against this backdrop, the inflationary impact of elevated energy prices, developments in the AI sector and the risk of further equity market liquidation, together with movements in bond yields and the dollar, will remain key drivers.

The risk of broader market deleveraging could weigh on gold in the short term, even as longer-term demand for portfolio diversification and protection against fiscal and geopolitical risks remains supportive. These competing forces are likely to shape trading as we approach a time of year when gold has delivered strong gains in recent years, although seasonal patterns offer no guarantee of a repeat.

Having rebounded from key technical support around USD 3,970, the tug of war between short-term momentum sellers and longer-term accumulators continues. In my view, this struggle largely explains the current lack of direction, with prices at levels where the next move could almost be decided by the flip of a coin.

This makes the technical levels particularly important, especially on the upside, where a sustained break above USD 4,070, followed by the more significant USD 4,230 resistance area, could force leveraged funds that have been reducing exposure in recent weeks back onto the buy side, potentially accelerating a recovery through short covering and renewed momentum buying.

Conversely, while a renewed move below USD 4,000 cannot be ruled out, I continue to believe that further weakness would attract demand from Chinese buyers, central banks and other longer-term investors looking to accumulate gold at more attractive levels. This underlying demand should help limit the downside, although it may not prevent temporary price overshoots during periods of forced liquidation.
